## Train, validation and test strategy

<!-- Task 4: the chosen split and its justification; what generalisation it represents; possible leakage or optimistic performance. -->
The Siamese network and the CNN used different data-splitting strategies to reflect their distinct tasks: the Siamese network was split by writer, while CNN was split by session. However, the proportions were kept consistent for both models: 60% for training, 20% for validation, and 20% for testing.

The Siamese network dataset was split at the writer level to ensure that no writer appeared in more than one set. A random image-level split was avoided, as this would allow the same writer to appear in both training and test sets, potentially producing an overly optimistic estimate of the model's generalisability. Testing on unseen writers provides a more meaningful assessment of the model's ability to verify handwriting from individuals not encountered during training. This evaluation reflects how the model would perform in a real-world setting; for example, verifying whether two documents were written by the same previously unseen individual. Image pairs were constructed independently within each split to prevent images from overlapping across datasets. 

A key limitation of this strategy is the small number of writers in this dataset. With only 20 writers in total, the split allocates just four writers each to the validation and test sets, making performance estimates noisy and sensitive to which writers were assigned to each set. Furthermore, the decision threshold was selected by maximising balanced accuracy on the validation set and is therefore optimised for those four specific writers, which may limit its generalisability to other unseen writers. 

The CNN dataset was split at the session-level. Since the task was writer-identification, the model had to be trained on images from all writers and evaluated on its performance on the sessions held out from training. This evaluation reflects the scenario of: given a set of handwritten images from a new session, how accurately can the model identify the writer? A limitation of this strategy is the small number of available sessions, with three used for training, one for validation and one for testing.

For both models, the test set was kept independent and used only for final evaluation, providing an unbiased assessment of model performance on the held-out data.
